## Introduction

In this notebook, we are reverse engineering the story, [As police struggle to solve homicides, Baltimore residents see an ‘open season for killing’](https://www.washingtonpost.com/investigations/as-police-struggle-to-solve-homicides-baltimore-residents-see-an-open-season-for-killing/2018/12/26/7ee561e4-fb24-11e8-8c9a-860ce2a8148f_story.html)

## Sentences to Engineer

In this notebook, we are reverse engineering five sentences from the story.

### Sentence 1

- **Sentence text**: [As Baltimore has seen a stunning surge of violence, with nearly a killing each day for the past three years in a city of 600,000, homicide arrests have plummeted. City police made an arrest in 41 percent of homicides in 2014; last year, the rate was just 27 percent, a 14 percentage point drop.]
- **Analysis summary**: [Write up two to three sentences describing the results of your analysis. Were you able to confirm the finding? If not, why not?] We were able to confirm the finding to be an average of 0.915 homicide arrests between 2015 and 2017 in Baltimore.

```{r}
homicide_with_cw <- homicide_data |>
  mutate(reported_date = ymd(reported_date)) |>
  mutate(bmore_since_2014 = case_when(
    state == "MD" & reported_date >= "2015-01-01" ~ "post-2015",
    .default = "pre-2015"))

# Display results of code below this codeblock

homicide_with_cw |>
  filter(bmore_since_2014 == "post-2015") |>
  summarise(total_uids = n()) / (365*3)
```

### Sentence 2

- **Sentence text**: [Of 50 of the nation’s largest cities, Baltimore is one of 34 where police now make homicide arrests less often than in 2014, according to a Washington Post analysis. In Chicago, the homicide arrest rate has dropped 21 percentage points, in Boston it has dropped 12 points and in St. Louis it is down 9.]

Homicide arrest rate in Baltimore between 2014 - 2016; Chicago homicide arrest; Boston homicide arrest rate

- **summary**: [Write up two to three sentences describing the results of your analysis. Were you able to confirm the finding? If not, why not?] **From brainstorming, the team came up with an idea to group_by city and then, the reported date. Through that, we were able to filter the years from 2007 to 2014. This was eventually followed up by counting each of the unique number of tags (UID) per year.**

```{r}
arrests_2014 <- ends_w_arrest_count |>
  filter(reported_year == ymd("2014-01-01") & total_uids >= 10) |>
  select(city, state, arrests_2014 = arrests)

arrests_2016 <- ends_w_arrest_count |>
  filter(reported_year == ymd("2016-01-01") & total_uids >= 10) |>
  select(city, state, arrests_2016 = arrests)

homicide_compare <- arrests_2014 |>
  inner_join(arrests_2016, join_by(city, state)) |>
  mutate(change = arrests_2016 - arrests_2014)

view(homicide_compare |> 
       filter(change < 0) |> 
       arrange(change))

nrow(homicide_compare)
homicide_compare |> filter(change < 0) |> nrow()
```

### Sentence 3

- **Sentence text**: [Baltimore is also one of 30 cities that have seen an increase in homicides in recent years, with the greatest raw number increase in killings of any city other than Chicago, which has four times the population. While homicide rates remain near historical lows in most American cities, Baltimore and Chicago are now both seeing murder tallies that rival the early 2000s.]
- **Analysis summary**: [Write up two to three sentences describing the results of your analysis. Were you able to confirm the finding? If not, why not?]

yes! While this still is certainly not the most efficient lol, it gets the job done. We were able to easily write off every one of their 2014 to the side (or just memorize it) and confirm the following numbers did not go up or down. We will find a more efficient way to do this later, but for now, it gets the job done. Had to back a couple of labs to remember floor_date, but got it nonetheless. Just had to group by city THEN reported date, then get a count of each unique number of tags (uid) with the amount per year.

```{r}

cleaned_up_homicide_data |> mutate(reported_date = ymd(reported_date)) |> mutate(reported_year = floor_date(reported_date, "year")) |>
  group_by(city, reported_year) |>
  summarise(total_uids = n()) |>
  arrange(city, reported_year)

colnames(hopefully_best_data)


uid_counts <- hopefully_best_data |>
  mutate(reported_year = floor_date(reported_date, "year")) |>
  group_by(city, state, reported_year) |>
  summarise(total_uids = n())

amount_of_uids_14 <- uid_counts |>
  filter(reported_year == ymd("2014-01-01")) |>
  select(city, state, amount_of_uids_14 = total_uids)

amount_of_uids_17 <- uid_counts |>
  filter(reported_year == ymd("2017-01-01")) |>
  select(city, state, amount_of_uids_17 = total_uids)

change_of_uids <- amount_of_uids_14 |>
  inner_join(amount_of_uids_17, join_by(city, state)) |>
  mutate(change = amount_of_uids_17 - amount_of_uids_14) |>
  filter(change > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(change))

change_of_uids
nrow(change_of_uids)
```

### Sentence 4

- **Sentence text**: [While there is evidence for and against a nationwide Ferguson effect — the theory that crime increased after 2014 as police faced more scrutiny following the shooting of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Mo. — in Baltimore there is an indisputable Freddie Gray effect. As violence in the city has risen since 2015, the likelihood of a killer being arrested has dropped precipitously. For most of the decade before 2015, Baltimore’s annual homicide arrest rate hovered at about 40 percent. Since 2015, the arrest rate hasn’t topped 30 percent in any year. And while most cities saw their arrest rates drop gradually, Baltimore’s decline was sudden — plummeting 15 percentage points in 2015, after Gray’s death, the largest single-year drop for any city already solving less than half its homicides.]

  **summary**: [Write up two to three sentences describing the results of your analysis. Were you able to confirm the finding? If not, why not?]

```{r}
#baltimore alone
ends_w_arrest_count |>
  filter(state == "MD") |>
  arrange(reported_year) |> 
  mutate(pct_arrst = (arrests / total_uids)*100)

#now other cities

ends_w_arrest_count |> group_by(city) |> 
  arrange(city, reported_year) |> 
  mutate(pct_arrst = (arrests / total_uids)*100) |> 
  filter(pct_arrst < 50)

ends_w_arrest_pct |>
  filter(city == "Sacramento") |>
  filter(reported_year == ymd("2014-01-01") | reported_year == ymd("2015-01-01")) |>
  select(city, reported_year, total_uids, arrests, arrest_rate)
```
